analysis.one_liner: Speeds generic drug approvals by limiting how brand-name drug patents block competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to speed generic drug competition was referred to committee and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change FDA rules so that certain patents brand-name drug makers hold on safety-program elements (called REMS) cannot delay approval of competing generic drugs. Under current law, a generic applicant must certify those patents, and the brand maker can sue, triggering a 30-month hold on approval. The bill removes that hold for REMS-related patents and limits brand makers to collecting money damages rather than court orders that keep generics off the market.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs subject to FDA safety-restricted distribution programs. Removing patent-based holds lets generic versions reach the market sooner, which typically means lower prices at the pharmacy and less out-of-pocket spending.

how_it_helps.text: Certifications of patents claiming REMS safety elements would have no effect on the approval date of a generic or biosimilar application, even ones pending or filed before enactment.
The bill negates the stay of approval that currently follows patent litigation, which can delay a generic's effective approval date while a lawsuit plays out.
In a patent-infringement suit over REMS-related intellectual property, the brand-name sponsor could seek only money damages, not an injunction blocking the competing product.
The bill preserves REMS safety requirements themselves and does not limit antitrust law, so the change targets competition-blocking uses of IP rather than safety oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers that hold patents on REMS program elements lose a tool that delays generic entry, and with it some period of extended monopoly pricing. Patent holders generally keep their patents but get a narrower remedy (damages instead of market exclusion).

drawbacks.text: Brand sponsors argue REMS patents protect real investments in building safe-distribution systems; stripping the injunction remedy weakens conventional patent enforcement for a category of biopharmaceutical IP and could reduce the incentive to develop safety programs for high-risk drugs.

Generics entering without resolving the underlying patent question could face more infringement litigation for damages after launch, and courts would have to work out how to value REMS-related IP in a damages-only regime.
The bill applies retroactively to applications submitted before enactment, which changes expectations for deals already made between brand and generic firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is faster generic entry on a set of drugs where distribution restrictions have been used to keep rivals out; the cost is a weaker patent remedy for brand sponsors in this specific context. The safety system itself (REMS) is left intact. The bill is narrow — it addresses only REMS-related patents, not the broader patent-thicket problem — but what it does is targeted at a documented delay mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on March 1, 2023, joined by Sen. Mike Braun, making it bipartisan from the start.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — and the Congress expired on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the status quo, including the ability to use REMS-related patents and litigation to delay generic competitors. Patients gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to speed generic approval where REMS-related patents are used to delay competition.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 1, 2023 and took no further action; the bill never received a markup or floor vote.

against.name: PhRMA and brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry with a stake in REMS-related patent remedies
against.what_they_did: The record contains no documented activity on this bill; industry opposition is inferred from the fact that the bill would remove a delay tool used by brand sponsors, not from any source in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction (one Democrat, one Republican), but no votes were ever taken, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill removes two levers brand sponsors use to delay generic entry on REMS-restricted drugs: the litigation stay and the injunction remedy. Losing those levers shortens their monopoly period on high-priced specialty drugs.

Faster, unencumbered approval of applications citing REMS-related patents lets generics reach the market sooner. The trade-off is that they could face damages suits after launch instead of pre-launch stays.

industries.industry: Consumers and payers of prescription drugs
industries.note: Earlier generic competition on REMS-restricted drugs, which tend to be expensive specialty medicines, would lower prices for patients, employers, and insurers.
